unit: Ch 1: GST in India: An Introduction
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Overview of Taxation System & Direct vs Indirect Taxes
explain: A tax is a mandatory financial charge imposed by the Government through law to fund public expenditure.
Direct tax is paid directly by the person on whom it is imposed and its burden cannot be shifted to another person.
Indirect tax is levied on goods or services where the immediate liability is on the supplier, but the burden is shifted to the consumer.
Direct tax is progressive as it depends on ability to pay, whereas indirect tax is regressive because everyone pays the same rate.

flow.title: Tax Burden Mechanism
steps: Government enacts tax law
Taxable event occurs
Direct tax paid directly by taxpayer
Indirect tax shifted to final consumer

topics.example: When you buy a packet of biscuits, the price includes GST paid by you to the shopkeeper, who deposits it with the Government.
remember: Direct tax cannot be shifted; Indirect tax burden is shifted to the final consumer.
mistakes: Assuming indirect tax is borne by the seller rather than passed on to the ultimate consumer.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of indirect taxes?
o: Based strictly on ability to pay
quiz.why: Indirect taxes are regressive because rich and poor consumers bear the exact same tax burden on purchasing goods/services.

quiz.q: Under which Constitutional Article is arbitrary levy or collection of tax prohibited?
quiz.why: Article 265 states that no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.

topics.title: Genesis of GST in India
explain: The GST concept was mooted in 2000 by the then Prime Minister, and a committee was set up to design the GST model.
In 2004, the FRBM Task Force strongly recommended a fully integrated national GST.
The 122nd Constitutional Amendment Bill was introduced in 2014 and passed by Parliament in 2015-2016.
It received Presidential assent on 8th September 2016 to become the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.
GST was formally launched in India on 1st July 2017 (and extended to Jammu & Kashmir on 8th July 2017).

flow.title: Timeline of GST Rollout
steps: 2000: Concept mooted by Prime Minister
2004: FRBM Task Force recommends GST
2014: 122nd Amendment Bill introduced
2016: 101st Amendment Act enacted
1st July 2017: GST implemented nationwide

topics.example: India transitioned from multiple state and central tax acts into a single unified GST law through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act.
remember: 122nd Bill became the 101st Amendment Act, 2016; GST launched on 1st July 2017 (J&K on 8th July 2017).
mistakes: Confusing the 122nd Amendment Bill number with the 101st Amendment Act number.

quiz.q: On which date was GST implemented across India (except J&K)?
quiz.why: GST was introduced across India on 1st July 2017, while J&K adopted it on 8th July 2017.

quiz.q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act paved the way for the introduction of GST in India?
quiz.why: The 122nd Amendment Bill was enacted as the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.

topics.title: Concept & Core Features of GST
explain: Destination-Based Consumption Tax: GST revenue accrues to the State/UT where goods/services are consumed.
Value Added Tax: Tax is charged only on the value added at each stage of the supply chain.
Continuous Chain of Credits: Every supplier gets set-off for input taxes paid on inward supplies.
No Tax Cascading: Since tax paid on inputs is credited, there is no levy of tax-on-tax.
Final Burden on Consumer: The ultimate consumer bears the entire GST charged by the last supplier.

flow.title: Value Addition & Credit Flow
steps: Supplier buys raw material with GST
Avails Input Tax Credit (ITC)
Adds value and calculates output GST
Pays Net GST = Output tax minus ITC
Consumer pays total price including final GST

topics.example: A manufacturer buys materials for Rs 1,00,000 paying Rs 18,000 GST. He adds value of Rs 11,200 and sells. He only pays Rs 2,016 net GST after claiming Rs 18,000 credit.
remember: GST is destination-based (consumption state gets revenue), whereas old VAT/CST was origin-based.
mistakes: Believing GST is charged on total turnover without giving credit for tax paid on purchases.

quiz.q: Why is GST called a 'destination-based' consumption tax?
o: Tax goes to the manufacturing State
Tax goes to the consuming State/UT
Tax goes exclusively to the Central Government
Tax is collected at the origin of goods
quiz.why: Under GST, revenue flows to the State or Union Territory where goods or services are consumed.

quiz.q: What prevents the cascading effect of taxes under the GST regime?
o: Continuous chain of Input Tax Credit
quiz.why: Continuous availability of credit for taxes paid on inputs eliminates tax-on-tax (cascading).

topics.title: Need for GST & Deficiencies in Pre-GST Regime
explain: In the old regime, CENVAT (Central Excise) applied at production, but credit was not available against State VAT.
Central Sales Tax (CST) on inter-State sales was origin-based and non-VATable, causing tax cascading.
Certain items like software and restaurant service suffered double taxation under both VAT and Service Tax.
Multiplicity of local taxes (Luxury tax, Entry tax, Entertainment tax) created high compliance costs.
Lack of uniform VAT rates and laws across different States made cross-border business cumbersome.

flow.title: Pre-GST Tax Cascading
steps: Manufacturer pays Central Excise duty
Excise included in taxable value for VAT
Inter-State sales attract non-setoff CST
State levies VAT on top of Excise and CST
Total price inflates due to tax-on-tax

topics.example: Before GST, if excise duty of Rs 125 was charged on a Rs 1,000 product, State VAT was charged on Rs 1,125, effectively levying tax on tax.
remember: Pre-GST deficiencies included double taxation, tax cascading, non-VATable CST, and multiplicity of taxes.
mistakes: Thinking CENVAT credit could be used to set off State VAT liabilities in the pre-GST era.

quiz.q: Which pre-GST tax was non-VATable and contributed heavily to tax cascading in inter-State trade?
quiz.why: CST was an origin-based, non-VATable tax; buyers could not claim input credit for CST paid.

quiz.q: Under the pre-GST regime, software transactions often suffered double taxation under which two taxes?
quiz.why: Software was treated as both a service (Service Tax) and goods (State VAT), triggering double taxation.

topics.title: Framework of GST in India (Dual GST Model)
explain: India adopted a Concurrent Dual GST Model where Centre and States simultaneously tax the supply of goods and services.
Intra-State Supply (within same State/UT with legislature) attracts CGST (Central GST) + SGST (State GST).
Intra-State Supply in a UT without legislature attracts CGST + UTGST.
Inter-State Supply (between two States/UTs or imports) attracts IGST (Integrated GST), levied and collected by Centre.
UTs with Legislature (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K) levy SGST, whereas UTs without Legislature levy UTGST.

flow.title: GST Structure Determination
steps: Check Supplier Location & Place of Supply
Same State / UT with Legislature -> CGST + SGST
Same UT without Legislature -> CGST + UTGST
Different States / UTs -> IGST

topics.example: A transaction within Delhi attracts CGST + SGST (Delhi has a legislature). A transaction within Ladakh attracts CGST + UTGST.
remember: IGST equals CGST plus SGST/UTGST. Delhi, Puducherry, and J&K enact their own SGST laws.
mistakes: Assuming Union Territories like Delhi or Puducherry levy UTGST instead of SGST.

quiz.q: Which combination of taxes applies to an intra-State supply made within the Union Territory of Ladakh?
quiz.why: Ladakh is a UT without a legislature, so intra-State supplies attract CGST + UTGST.

quiz.q: Who levies and collects Integrated GST (IGST) on inter-State transactions?
quiz.why: IGST is levied and collected by the Central Government on all inter-State supplies and apportioned to States.

topics.title: Registration Thresholds, Composition Scheme & Credit Utilization
explain: Threshold limit for GST registration is Rs 10 Lakhs for Special Category States (Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura).
Threshold limit is Rs 20 Lakhs for goods/services in Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Puducherry, Telangana.
Threshold limit is Rs 40 Lakhs for exclusive suppliers of goods making only intra-State supplies in all other States.
Composition Scheme provides relief to small businesses by allowing payment of tax at low flat rates with minimal formalities.
Order of ITC utilization: IGST credit must be fully exhausted first against IGST, CGST, SGST/UTGST. CGST credit cannot pay SGST and vice versa.

flow.title: Order of Input Tax Credit (ITC) Utilization
steps: Set off IGST credit against IGST output tax
Set off remaining IGST credit against CGST/SGST output
Set off CGST credit against CGST, then IGST
Set off SGST credit against SGST, then IGST
Never set off CGST credit against SGST or vice versa

topics.example: If a trader has Rs 900 CGST credit, he can set it off against his Rs 1,080 CGST output tax liability, but cannot use it for SGST.
remember: Thresholds for goods: Rs 10L (4 Manipur/Mizoram/Nagaland/Tripura), Rs 20L (6 States/UTs), Rs 40L (Rest of India).
Cross-utilization between CGST and SGST/UTGST is strictly prohibited.
mistakes: Attempting to pay SGST output tax using available CGST credit.

quiz.q: What is the threshold limit for GST registration for an exclusive supplier of goods making intra-State supplies in Delhi?
quiz.why: For exclusive intra-State suppliers of goods in States/UTs like Delhi, the registration threshold is Rs 40 Lakhs.

quiz.q: Which set-off combination of Input Tax Credit is NOT permitted under GST?
quiz.why: CGST credit can never be cross-utilized to pay SGST output tax, and vice versa.

topics.title: GST IT Ecosystem: GSTN, E-Way Bill, IRP & GSPs/ASPs
explain: GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network) manages the common electronic portal (www.gst.gov.in) for registration, returns, and IGST settlement.
E-way bill portal (www.ewaybillgst.gov.in) managed by NIC generates electronic documents evidencing movement of goods.
Invoice Registration Portal (IRP) handles e-invoicing for businesses with aggregate turnover exceeding Rs 5 Crore in any year from 2017-18.
GST Suvidha Providers (GSPs) and Application Service Providers (ASPs) help taxpayers integrate ERPs and automate compliance.

flow.title: GST Digital Architecture
steps: Business generates invoice on ERP
Uploads invoice to IRP for e-invoicing (if > Rs 5Cr)
Generates E-way bill on NIC portal for transport
Files monthly returns on GSTN Common Portal
GSTN matches tax payments and computes IGST settlement

topics.example: A company with Rs 10 Crore turnover reports invoices on the IRP website, creates E-way bills for delivery trucks, and files returns on GSTN.
remember: GSTN portal = www.gst.gov.in; E-Way Bill portal = www.ewaybillgst.gov.in; E-invoicing applies if turnover > Rs 5 Crore.
mistakes: Confusing the Common GST Portal (GSTN) with the E-way bill portal managed by NIC.

quiz.q: Which entity manages the Common GST Electronic Portal (www.gst.gov.in)?
o: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC)
quiz.why: GSTN is a wholly government-owned company set up to manage the shared IT infrastructure for GST.

quiz.q: What is the turnover threshold above which a registered business is required to issue e-invoices?
quiz.why: Businesses with an aggregate turnover exceeding Rs 5 Crore in any preceding financial year from 2017-18 must generate e-invoices.

topics.title: Taxability of Specific Goods, Subsumed Taxes & Compensation Cess
explain: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is constitutionally outside GST; it attracts State Excise Duty and CST/VAT.
5 Petroleum products (Crude oil, Diesel, Petrol, ATF, Natural Gas) are temporarily outside GST until notified by GST Council.
Tobacco is subject to BOTH GST and Central Excise Duty.
Opium, Indian hemp, and narcotic drugs are subject to BOTH GST and State Excise Duties.
Taxes subsumed: Excise duty, Service tax, CST, VAT, Luxury tax, Entry tax, State Entertainment tax. Taxes not subsumed: Customs duty, Stamp duty, Property tax, Local body Entertainment tax.
Compensation Cess was levied on luxury and demerit goods to compensate States for revenue loss; now phased out.

flow.title: Tax Applicability Matrix
steps: Alcohol for Human Consumption -> State Excise + VAT/CST
5 Petroleum Products -> Central Excise + VAT/CST
Tobacco -> GST + Central Excise Duty
Narcotics/Opium -> GST + State Excise Duty
Demerit Goods -> GST + Compensation Cess

topics.example: Purchasing petrol at a fuel station attracts Central Excise Duty and State VAT, whereas purchasing a cigarette pack attracts GST plus Central Excise Duty.
remember: Tobacco = GST + Central Excise; Alcohol = Outside GST (State Excise + VAT); Local body entertainment tax is NOT subsumed.
mistakes: Believing that local body entertainment taxes were subsumed under GST.

quiz.q: Which of the following items is completely outside the realm of GST by constitutional definition?
quiz.why: Article 366(12A) explicitly excludes alcoholic liquor for human consumption from the definition of GST.

quiz.q: Which tax was NOT subsumed into GST?
o: Entertainment tax levied by local bodies
quiz.why: Entertainment taxes levied by local bodies (panchayats/municipalities) were retained and not subsumed into GST.

topics.title: Benefits of GST to Economy, Trade & Industry
explain: Unified National Market: Removes interstate trade barriers, standardizing tax rates and procedures across India.
Boost to Make in India: Parity between domestic goods and imported goods (IGST equivalent to CGST+SGST) enhances competitiveness.
Export Promotion: Full set-off of input taxes ensures export of goods without exporting taxes, boosting balance of payments.
Mitigation of Cascading Effect: Seamless flow of Input Tax Credit ensures tax neutrality across the entire supply chain.
Ease of Doing Business: Uniform online procedures, reduced human interaction, auto-populated returns, and simplified compliance.

flow.title: Economic Impact of GST
steps: Implementation of unified tax rates
Removal of cascading taxes via seamless ITC
Lower production cost and reduced prices
Increased consumption and manufacturing
Boost to GDP, exports, and employment

topics.example: An Indian exporter claims a 90% provisional refund of input tax within 7 days, improving cash flows and international price competitiveness.
remember: GST makes the supply chain tax neutral by allowing seamless ITC across state borders.
mistakes: Thinking GST increased overall prices by imposing taxes on tax.

quiz.q: How does GST provide tax parity between locally produced goods and imported goods?
o: By exempting local goods from tax
By levying IGST on imports equivalent to CGST + SGST
By imposing custom duties on local goods
quiz.why: Imported goods attract IGST, which is roughly equal to CGST plus SGST, putting local and imported goods on equal footing.

quiz.q: What benefit does GST provide to exporters to prevent exporting taxes?
o: Seamless input tax credit and provisional refund
quiz.why: Under GST, exporters receive refunds on input taxes paid, ensuring only the cost of goods is exported, not the tax.

topics.title: Constitutional Provisions Relating to GST & GST Council
explain: Article 246A: Empowers Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on GST; Parliament has exclusive power over inter-State supply.
Article 269A: IGST on inter-State supply is levied/collected by Central Govt and apportioned between Centre and States. Imports are deemed inter-State supply.
Article 366(12A): Defines GST as any tax on supply of goods, services, or both, except alcoholic liquor for human consumption.
Article 366(26A): Services means anything other than goods.

Article 279A: Empowers President to constitute GST Council (Chairperson: Union Finance Minister). Decisions require 3/4th weighted majority (Centre = 1/3 vote, States combined = 2/3 vote; Quorum = 1/2 of members).

flow.title: GST Council Decision Making Process
steps: President constitutes Council under Article 279A
Ensure Quorum (at least 1/2 members present)
Central Vote Weightage = 1/3rd of total cast
All States Vote Weightage = 2/3rds of total cast
Decision passed if weighted majority >= 3/4th (75%)

topics.example: If the Central Government opposes a tax rate change supported by all States, the proposal cannot pass because 2/3rd (66.67%) is less than the required 3/4th (75%) majority.
remember: Article 246A gives power to levy GST; Article 269A governs IGST; Article 279A creates GST Council.
GST Council voting weightage: Centre = 1/3rd, States = 2/3rds; Decision threshold = 3/4th (75%).
mistakes: Assuming the Union Finance Minister can single-handedly override all State Finance Ministers in a GST Council vote.

quiz.q: Which Article of the Constitution gives concurrent power to Parliament and State Legislatures to levy GST?
quiz.why: Article 246A was inserted by the 101st CAA to grant concurrent powers to Centre and States for imposing GST.

quiz.q: What is the required weighted majority for passing any decision in a meeting of the GST Council under Article 279A?
quiz.why: Every decision of the GST Council requires a majority of not less than three-fourths (75%) of the weighted votes present and voting.
